Room temperature dissolving cellulose with a metal salt hydrate-based deep eutectic solvent
<::logo: Unknown Check for updates A square button with a red and yellow bookmark symbol within a blue circle, above the text "Check for updates".::>
Zhihan Tong, Juan Meng, Shi Liu, Yongzhuang Liu, Suqing Zeng, Lei Wang, Qinqin Xia*, Haipeng Yu*
Key Laboratory of Bio-based Material Science and Technology of Ministry of Education, Northeast Forestry University, Harbin 150040, Heilongjiang, China
ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Aqueous solutions Biorefining Cellulose Deep eutectic solvents DFT calculations Solubility Sustainable chemistry

ABSTRACT Abundant and renewable cellulose is a potential candidate for petroleum-derived synthetic polymers. However, the efficient dissolution of this material is problematic because of the high cost, severe reaction condition (e.g., high temperature) and environmentally unfriendly (e.g., toxic reagents, and solvent recyclability). Herein, to realize the room temperature dissolution of cellulose with an inexpensive and eco-friendly solvent, we design a novel low-cost deep eutectic solvent that is composed of zinc chloride, water and phosphoric acid for the efficient dissolution of cellulose. This solvent is featured as having both the superior hydrogen bonding acidity and the hydrogen bonding basicity, and thus can act as a hydrogen bond molecular scissors to cleave the hydrogen bonds within cellulose. In this process, microcrystalline cellulose can be easily dissolved in the solvent at room temperature with a dissolution ratio up to 15 wt%. The dissolved cellulose can also be recovered without any derivatization. The universality, recyclability and pilot production of dissolving cellulose using this solvent are also demonstrated. This work provides a new strategy for the design of novel deep eutectic solvent capable of disrupting the hydrogen bonds of cellulose under mild conditions.

1. Introduction As a readily available, naturally occurring biopolymer, cellulose can be considered an almost inexhaustible resource based on the annual growth of 1.5 × 10¹² tons of this substance (Klemm et al., 2005; Ragauskas et al., 2006). The dissolution process is to tune the structure of cellulose molecules from the microscope, and construct a series of new types of fibers, hydrogels, membranes and artificial silk materials (Jia et al., 2019; Pang et al., 2021; Tardy et al., 2021), opening up a way to efficiently utilize cellulose resources (Zhu et al., 2021). Cellulose is typically bound to hemicellulose and lignin within the cell walls of plants (Berglund and Burgert, 2018). The robust semicrystalline struc-ture of cellulose via extensive hydrogen bonds (H-bonds) renders it insoluble in water and many organic solvents, which renders the sub-sequent processes difficult (Martinez, 2016). For these reasons, there is significant interest in the development of new, efficient and environ-mentally friendly solvents for the dissolution of cellulose.

Currently, both the derivatizing and non-derivatizing solvents are commonly used for cellulose dissolution (Yang et al., 2021). Derivatiz- ing solvents (e.g., copper ammonia solution, cadmium/ethylenediamine solution, NaOH/CS2 and carbamate solvent) usually cause significant degradation of the cellulose structure, and cannot be efficiently recycled (Van de Vyver et al., 2011). The development of highly effective, non- derivatizing solvents for cellulose dissolution has thus been of interest for many years. Ionic liquids as the non-derivatizing solvents (De Oli- veira and Rinaldi, 2015; Swatloski et al., 2002) are typically composed of large organic cations and low charge density anions (Zhao et al., 2013). During the cellulose dissolution process, the anions can form strong H-bonds with the hydroxyl groups in cellulose chains while the cations primarily provide steric hindrance (Zhang et al., 2016). Ionic liquids are found to readily dissolve cellulose (Ferreira et al., 2019; Lethesh et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2012) but are still costly and difficult to recycle, which limit their industrial applications. These include tetrabuty- lammonium hydroxide (TBAH), tetrabutylphosphonium hydroxide (TBPH) (Nguyen et al., 2019), tetrabutylammonium acetate/dimethyl sulfoxide (TBAA/DMSO) (Huang et al., 2016), TBAH/DMSO (Chen et al., 2018), TBAH/urea, and others. These compounds are similar, in that they contain superbase cations that can attack the reducing ends of cellulose chains to initiate free radical reactions, thus disrupting the ordered structure of the cellulose. Subsequent to this, electron donor- acceptor coordination reactions can proceed (Li et al., 2020). The sol- vation effect of small molecules promotes the dissociation of free ions and facilitates ion mobility, while urea adjusts the amphiphilicity of the system, thereby improving the solubility of cellulose. However, the toxicity issue of these compounds tends to limit their widespread applications.

Alternatively, inorganic molten salt hydrates are reported with similar characteristics to ionic liquids and are of special interest due to their ease of preparation and low cost (Sen et al., 2013). As an example, zinc chloride hydrate (ZnCl2·nH2O) can be used to directly process cellulose within the formula range 2 < n < 4 (Bodachivskyi et al., 2019; Wilcox et al., 2014). Its similar compound formula (which can also be considered to exist as [Zn(OH2)6]2+ [ZnCl4]2−) can dissolve cellulose. However, the solubility of cellulose in such inorganic salt hydrates is very low (<5 wt%) and needs high temperature (>80 °C), causing energy consumption and partially hydrolysis. Therefore, it is critical to design a facile and environmentally friendly solvent to effectively dissolve cellulose under mild conditions while at the same time reducing the excessive hydrolysis, thus requiring a unique balance between dissolution and hydrolysis.

A metal salt hydrate-based deep eutectic solvent (DES IV) that in- volves metal salt hydrate (as H-bond acceptor) in combination with various H-bond donors (e.g., acid, urea, amide) is a promising alterna- tive solvent for dissolving cellulose due to its low cost and high H-bond accepting ability (Chen and Mu, 2019; Jiang et al., 2019; Meng et al., 2021; Sirviö, 2019; Sirviö and Heiskanen, 2017; Wang et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2018, 2019). Here, we intend to design such a type of solvent that can act as "Hydrogen bond molecular scissors" (Luo et al., 2020) to realize the room temperature dissolution of cellulose. Based on the concept of DES IV, a combination of metal salt hydrates and polyacids is hypothesized under certain conditions to improve the dissolution ca- pacity of the mixture (Scheme 1). Water acts as an essential constituent to regulate the behavior of the ions and the catalytic effect. The detri- mental effect of excess hydration on the solvent effect is a concern. For this reason, density functional theory (DFT) calculations are employed

to study the internal supramolecular interactions among the constituent species at the atomic level. The goal was to obtain an in-depth under- standing of the solvation mechanism, combined with an experimental optimization to determine the best performing room temperature cel- lulose solvent.

## 2. Experimental ### 2.1. Cellulose feedstocks Four types of cellulose were selected as the feedstocks for the dissolution experiments. Microcrystalline cellulose (MCC, 25 µm) was purchased from the Aladdin Reagent Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China), wood cellulose was extracted from poplar wood using the sodium chlorite method (see Supplementary Note S1), bleached softwood pulp was purchased from the Jiali Trade Co. Ltd. (Liaoning, China) and commercial degreasing cotton was obtained from the Yanggu JYG Hygiene & Health Factory (Shandong, China). All these cellulose feedstocks were characterized with regard to degree of polymerization (DP), average molecular weight, α-cellulose content and crystallinity.

2.2. Preparation of the DESs Zinc chloride and phosphoric acid (purity 85%) were purchased from the Kermel Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. (Tianjin, China). Zinc chloride, water and phosphoric acid were mixed at molar ratios of 1:x:y (x = 2.5, 3, 3.5 or 4; y = 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 or 1.0) and stirred at room temperature (23–26 °C, 40%RH) for 5 min. The resulting solvents are referred to herein as MSA-x-y.

2.3. Dissolution of cellulose Trials involving the room temperature dissolution of cellulose were initiated by adding a specific mass of cellulose (5–17 wt%) to a 100 mL round-bottomed flask together with 20 g of the solvent, followed by stirring at 600 rpm. Samples were taken at intervals of 10 min to observe the dimensions (e.g., length, width) and shapes (e.g., fiber or particle) of cellulose using a polarized light microscopy (Smart-POL, Chongqing Optec Instrument Co. Ltd., Chongqing, China). The dissolution time can be considered as the useful information translated into dissolution efficiency.

## 2.4. DFT calculations Based on the role of H-bond donor-acceptor pairing in DES, three metal salt hydrates were evaluated for the synthesis of new solvents. LiCl·3H₂O, MgCl₂·3H₂O, ZnCl₂·3H₂O are denoted as MS1, MS2, MS3, respectively. The structure of cellobiose and molecular interactions between the solvent and cellobiose in this work were studied using the Gaussian 16 package, with all samples optimized at the M06-2X/6-311+G** level. Frequency analyses were carried out for the optimized structures to verify energy minima and provide zero-point energy corrections. Thermochemical characteristics were also assessed to ensure consistency and reproducibility. To eliminate the dispersion effect, the empirical dispersion keyword = gd3 was added to the route section and the calculations were optimized without symmetry restrictions. MultiWFN code (Lu and Chen, 2012) was used to analyze the calculation results.

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Designing a H-bond molecular scissors solvent The dissolution of cellulose depends on the free energy change in the mixed system, and this value is the sum of enthalpy and entropy changes. The driving force for dissolution is always an increase in the absolute value of entropy (Zhang et al., 2019). Entropy-driven dissolution reactions are of theoretical importance because free energy is the driving force for chemical changes. Therefore the interaction energy of cellobiose (a simple model for cellulose) was first analyzed by DFT calculations. The theoretical H-bonding interaction energy between cellobiose units was determined to be –15.05 kcal mol⁻¹ (Supplementary Fig. S1), while the glucosidic bond dissociation energy of cellobiose was up to 138.08 kcal mol⁻¹ (Fig. 1A). Ishida previously calculated the intermolecular interaction energies of cellulose at 25 °C, including the effects of reducing end groups, internal groups and non-reducing end groups in the gas phase as well as in water and ionic liquids, and obtained values in the range of –16.8 to –25.5 kcal mol⁻¹ (Ishida, 2020). The criterion for selecting solvents was that the interaction energy between the solvent and cellobiose should be greater than that between the cellobiose units but should not exceed the glucosidic bond dissociation energy, so as to achieve an efficient dissolution and simultaneously avoid excessive hydrolysis (Cho et al., 2011). Considering the complexity of cellulose-solvent interactions, the lower limit of the interaction energy for efficiently dissolving cellulose should be higher than 25.5 kcal mol⁻¹.

Three metal salt hydrates were evaluated for the synthesis of new solvents by DFT analysis, including the LiCl·3H₂O (symbolized herein as MS1), MgCl₂·3H₂O (MS2) and ZnCl₂·3H₂O (MS3). Three acids were also assessed: oxalic acid (A1), acetic acid (A2) and phosphoric acid (A3). The interaction energies of the combinations of these compounds were calculated by DFT (Supplementary Fig. S2) and are summarized in Fig. 1B, from which it is evident that only the H-bonding interaction energy of the MS3A3 pair met the criterion of being larger than 25.5 kcal mol⁻¹. The interaction energies between each solvent combination and cellobiose were calculated based on DFT (Supplementary Fig. S3) and are provided in Supplementary Table S1. The MS3A3 system had the highest interaction energy with cellobiose (−29.44 kcal mol⁻¹), indicating that it could be the most effective solvent according to the criterion of selecting solvent (Supplementary Fig. S4). In addition, the pKa value of the MS3A3 (Supplementary Fig. S6) is significantly lower than those of the majority of the other combinations and of any of the pure acids (Supplementary Table S2). This result suggests that MS3A3 has more numerous dissociated hydrogen ions, facilitating to improve the ability of solvent to destroy intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonds within cellulose. On this basis, the MS3A3 system was considered an ideal solvent to test the aforementioned hypothesis.

The atoms in molecules (AIM) theory is often employed to quantify the H-bond interactions at bond critical point (BCPs) in terms of electron density (ρ, 0.002–0.035 au) and the Laplacian of the electron density (∇²ρ, 0.024–0.139 au). The ρ value indicates the bond strength while the ∇²ρ value indicates the bond type (that is, H-bond, ionic bond or van der Waals force). In our solvent, the hydrogen atom of hydroxyl group in phosphoric acid molecule can form H-bonds with Cl⁻ ion (ρ = 0.0386 au; ∇²ρ = 0.0752 au) with a distance of 1.995 Å (Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. S4). This promotes the release of Cl⁻ ions from the Zn²⁺

ions, such that the distance between Zn2+ and Cl- ions is increased from 2.464 to 2.801 Å. Simultaneously, the Zn2+ ions coordinate with the hydroxyl groups of the phosphoric acid. The resulting interatomic dis- tances are within the range of less than 3.5 Å over which H-bonding can occur.

Fig. 1C and Supplementary Fig. S4 exhibit the topological graph of the MS3A3-cellobiose system by AIM analysis. Table 1 summarizes the ρ and ∇²ρ values for all BCPs between MS3A3 and cellobiose. The calculation results indicate that H⁺ ions are released from the phosphoric acid that forms strong H-bonds with O atoms in C₆-OH groups (ρ = 0.0811 au, ∇²ρ = 0.1382 au). Meanwhile, the distance between Zn²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions also increases to 3.793 Å, indicating that the Cl⁻ ions are no longer tightly bonded to the Zn²⁺ ions, thus, these Cl⁻ ions subsequently form H-bonding interactions with C₁-H groups in the cellobiose as well as C₃-H, C₅-H and C₆-H moieties, leading to selectively compete or wrap H-bond of cellulose itself. It also adjusts the amphiphilicity of the solvent, thereby increasing the ability to dissolve cellulose. At the same time, Zn²⁺ ions form coordination bonds with the oxygen atoms in C₆-OH groups in the cellobiose (ρ = 0.0458 au, ∇²ρ = 0.2021 au) and water molecules form H-bonds with the cellobiose, which also facilitate the cellulose to dissolve. In addition, the ρ and ∇²ρ values in the cellobiose itself both decrease, indicating that the MS3A3 is theoretically capable of dissolving cellulose and is superior to MS3 and A3 alone (Supplementary Table S3).

3.4. Demonstrations of pilot production and recyclable dissolution In the process of industrial production of cellulose dissolution, the desired solvent must have the characteristics of recyclability, good universality, pilot production, high efficiency, and low cost. In the solvent system that we designed, the MS3A3 demonstrates excellent recyclability. Even after recycling, the MS3A3 maintained its high ability to dissolve cellulose (original solvent: 15 wt%; after 1 time: 15 wt%, Fig. 4A and Supplementary Fig. S11). After reusing the MS3A3 for five times, the dissolved ratio of cellulose was 5 wt%, indicating the effect of the H-bond molecular scissors of the MS3A3 was retained even after being recycled and reused. In addition, the maximum dissolution ratios of other cellulose feedstocks with different molecular weights were also assessed (Fig. 4B), and in each case the extent of dissolution was considered satisfactory (Supplementary Fig. S12). Although the DP of cellulose feedstock increased from 183 to 2243, the dissolution time and the viscosity of solution did not change greatly (Supplementary Table S7), which suggests the broad applicability of MS3A3 for dissolving various types of cellulose. Fig. 4C presents photographic images of a pilot production experiment of dissolving 550 g of MCC with the MSA-3-0.6 at room temperature, demonstrating its suitability not only in the laboratory uses but also at the pilot scale. The cost effectiveness and minimal energy consumption associated with dissolution using the MSA-3-0.6 solvent indicates that this system could compete with the NaOH/urea system and superior to many other solvents (Fig. 4D and Supplementary Table S8). All these results support that the new solvent has a very broad and quite optimistic application prospects.

## 4. Conclusion In summary, with the assistance of DFT calculations, a new solvent comprising zinc chloride, water and phosphoric acid (at molar ratio of 1:3:0.6) was successfully designed for the room temperature dissolution of cellulose. The data show that ZnCl2·3H2O and H3PO4 produce a new DES with strong H-bond donor-acceptor properties in which with water acts as an intermediate mediator to provide polar environment and avoid cellulose hydrolysis. This solvent has a protonation property and a characteristic of both having strong H-bonding acidity and basicity to achieve in efficiently dissolving cellulose (15 wt%). The newly developed solvent also has excellent universality, which can successfully dissolve the cellulose from various sources (e.g., microcrystalline, pulp cellulose, wood cellulose and cotton linter) at room temperature. This dissolution process did not phosphorylate the cellulose, although the cellulose recovered from solution showed a change in crystal structure from type I to II. In summary, this tailored solvent has a broad and quite optimistic application prospects.

However, the efficient dissolution of this material is problematic because of the high cost, severe reaction condition (e.g., high temperature) and environmentally unfriendly (e.g., toxic reagents, and solvent recyclability). Herein, to realize the room temperature dissolution of cellulose with an inexpensive and eco-friendly solvent, we design a novel low-cost deep eutectic solvent that is composed of zinc chloride, water and phosphoric acid for the efficient dissolution of cellulose. This solvent is featured as having both the superior hydrogen bonding acidity and the hydrogen bonding basicity, and thus can act as a hydrogen bond molecular scissors to cleave the hydrogen bonds within cellulose. In this process, microcrystalline cellulose can be easily dissolved in the solvent at room temperature with a dissolution ratio up to 15 wt%. The dissolved cellulose can also be recovered without any derivatization. The universality, recyclability and pilot production of dissolving cellulose using this solvent are also demonstrated. This work provides a new strategy for the design of novel deep eutectic solvent capable of disrupting the hydrogen bonds of cellulose under mild conditions. 1. Introduction As a readily available, naturally occurring biopolymer, cellulose can be considered an almost inexhaustible resource based on the annual growth of 1.5 × 10¹² tons of this substance (Klemm et al., 2005; Ragauskas et al., 2006). The dissolution process is to tune the structure of cellulose molecules from the microscope, and construct a series of new types of fibers, hydrogels, membranes and artificial silk materials (Jia et al., 2019; Pang et al., 2021; Tardy et al., 2021), opening up a way to efficiently utilize cellulose resources (Zhu et al., 2021). Cellulose is typically bound to hemicellulose and lignin within the cell walls of plants (Berglund and Burgert, 2018). The robust semicrystalline struc-ture of cellulose via extensive hydrogen bonds (H-bonds) renders it insoluble in water and many organic solvents, which renders the sub-sequent processes difficult (Martinez, 2016). For these reasons, there is significant interest in the development of new, efficient and environ-mentally friendly solvents for the dissolution of cellulose. Currently, both the derivatizing and non-derivatizing solvents are commonly used for cellulose dissolution (Yang et al., 2021). Derivatiz- ing solvents (e.g., copper ammonia solution, cadmium/ethylenediamine solution, NaOH/CS2 and carbamate solvent) usually cause significant degradation of the cellulose structure, and cannot be efficiently recycled (Van de Vyver et al., 2011). The development of highly effective, non- derivatizing solvents for cellulose dissolution has thus been of interest for many years. Ionic liquids as the non-derivatizing solvents (De Oli- veira and Rinaldi, 2015; Swatloski et al., 2002) are typically composed of large organic cations and low charge density anions (Zhao et al., 2013). During the cellulose dissolution process, the anions can form strong H-bonds with the hydroxyl groups in cellulose chains while the cations primarily provide steric hindrance (Zhang et al., 2016). Ionic liquids are found to readily dissolve cellulose (Ferreira et al., 2019; Lethesh et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2012) but are still costly and difficult to recycle, which limit their industrial applications. These include tetrabuty- lammonium hydroxide (TBAH), tetrabutylphosphonium hydroxide (TBPH) (Nguyen et al., 2019), tetrabutylammonium acetate/dimethyl sulfoxide (TBAA/DMSO) (Huang et al., 2016), TBAH/DMSO (Chen et al., 2018), TBAH/urea, and others. These compounds are similar, in that they contain superbase cations that can attack the reducing ends of cellulose chains to initiate free radical reactions, thus disrupting the ordered structure of the cellulose. Subsequent to this, electron donor- acceptor coordination reactions can proceed (Li et al., 2020). The sol- vation effect of small molecules promotes the dissociation of free ions and facilitates ion mobility, while urea adjusts the amphiphilicity of the system, thereby improving the solubility of cellulose. However, the toxicity issue of these compounds tends to limit their widespread applications. Alternatively, inorganic molten salt hydrates are reported with similar characteristics to ionic liquids and are of special interest due to their ease of preparation and low cost (Sen et al., 2013). As an example, zinc chloride hydrate (ZnCl2·nH2O) can be used to directly process cellulose within the formula range 2 < n < 4 (Bodachivskyi et al., 2019; Wilcox et al., 2014). Its similar compound formula (which can also be considered to exist as [Zn(OH2)6]2+ [ZnCl4]2−) can dissolve cellulose. However, the solubility of cellulose in such inorganic salt hydrates is very low (<5 wt%) and needs high temperature (>80 °C), causing energy consumption and partially hydrolysis. Therefore, it is critical to design a facile and environmentally friendly solvent to effectively dissolve cellulose under mild conditions while at the same time reducing the excessive hydrolysis, thus requiring a unique balance between dissolution and hydrolysis. A metal salt hydrate-based deep eutectic solvent (DES IV) that in- volves metal salt hydrate (as H-bond acceptor) in combination with various H-bond donors (e.g., acid, urea, amide) is a promising alterna- tive solvent for dissolving cellulose due to its low cost and high H-bond accepting ability (Chen and Mu, 2019; Jiang et al., 2019; Meng et al., 2021; Sirviö, 2019; Sirviö and Heiskanen, 2017; Wang et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2018, 2019). Here, we intend to design such a type of solvent that can act as "Hydrogen bond molecular scissors" (Luo et al., 2020) to realize the room temperature dissolution of cellulose. Based on the concept of DES IV, a combination of metal salt hydrates and polyacids is hypothesized under certain conditions to improve the dissolution ca- pacity of the mixture (Scheme 1). Water acts as an essential constituent to regulate the behavior of the ions and the catalytic effect. The detri- mental effect of excess hydration on the solvent effect is a concern. For this reason, density functional theory (DFT) calculations are employed to study the internal supramolecular interactions among the constituent species at the atomic level. The goal was to obtain an in-depth under- standing of the solvation mechanism, combined with an experimental optimization to determine the best performing room temperature cel- lulose solvent. ## 2. Results and discussion 3.1. Designing a H-bond molecular scissors solvent The dissolution of cellulose depends on the free energy change in the mixed system, and this value is the sum of enthalpy and entropy changes. The driving force for dissolution is always an increase in the absolute value of entropy (Zhang et al., 2019). Entropy-driven dissolution reactions are of theoretical importance because free energy is the driving force for chemical changes. Therefore the interaction energy of cellobiose (a simple model for cellulose) was first analyzed by DFT calculations. The theoretical H-bonding interaction energy between cellobiose units was determined to be –15.05 kcal mol⁻¹ (Supplementary Fig. S1), while the glucosidic bond dissociation energy of cellobiose was up to 138.08 kcal mol⁻¹ (Fig. 1A). Ishida previously calculated the intermolecular interaction energies of cellulose at 25 °C, including the effects of reducing end groups, internal groups and non-reducing end groups in the gas phase as well as in water and ionic liquids, and obtained values in the range of –16.8 to –25.5 kcal mol⁻¹ (Ishida, 2020). The criterion for selecting solvents was that the interaction energy between the solvent and cellobiose should be greater than that between the cellobiose units but should not exceed the glucosidic bond dissociation energy, so as to achieve an efficient dissolution and simultaneously avoid excessive hydrolysis (Cho et al., 2011). Considering the complexity of cellulose-solvent interactions, the lower limit of the interaction energy for efficiently dissolving cellulose should be higher than 25.5 kcal mol⁻¹. Three metal salt hydrates were evaluated for the synthesis of new solvents by DFT analysis, including the LiCl·3H₂O (symbolized herein as MS1), MgCl₂·3H₂O (MS2) and ZnCl₂·3H₂O (MS3). Three acids were also assessed: oxalic acid (A1), acetic acid (A2) and phosphoric acid (A3). The interaction energies of the combinations of these compounds were calculated by DFT (Supplementary Fig. S2) and are summarized in Fig. 1B, from which it is evident that only the H-bonding interaction energy of the MS3A3 pair met the criterion of being larger than 25.5 kcal mol⁻¹. The interaction energies between each solvent combination and cellobiose were calculated based on DFT (Supplementary Fig. S3) and are provided in Supplementary Table S1. The MS3A3 system had the highest interaction energy with cellobiose (−29.44 kcal mol⁻¹), indicating that it could be the most effective solvent according to the criterion of selecting solvent (Supplementary Fig. S4). The atoms in molecules (AIM) theory is often employed to quantify the H-bond interactions at bond critical point (BCPs) in terms of electron density (ρ, 0.002–0.035 au) and the Laplacian of the electron density (∇²ρ, 0.024–0.139 au). The ρ value indicates the bond strength while the ∇²ρ value indicates the bond type (that is, H-bond, ionic bond or van der Waals force). In our solvent, the hydrogen atom of hydroxyl group in phosphoric acid molecule can form H-bonds with Cl⁻ ion (ρ = 0.0386 au; ∇²ρ = 0.0752 au) with a distance of 1.995 Å (Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. S4). This promotes the release of Cl⁻ ions from the Zn²⁺ ions, such that the distance between Zn2+ and Cl- ions is increased from 2.464 to 2.801 Å. Simultaneously, the Zn2+ ions coordinate with the hydroxyl groups of the phosphoric acid. The resulting interatomic dis- tances are within the range of less than 3.5 Å over which H-bonding can occur. Fig. 1C and Supplementary Fig. S4 exhibit the topological graph of the MS3A3-cellobiose system by AIM analysis. Table 1 summarizes the ρ and ∇²ρ values for all BCPs between MS3A3 and cellobiose. The calculation results indicate that H⁺ ions are released from the phosphoric acid that forms strong H-bonds with O atoms in C₆-OH groups (ρ = 0.0811 au, ∇²ρ = 0.1382 au). Meanwhile, the distance between Zn²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions also increases to 3.793 Å, indicating that the Cl⁻ ions are no longer tightly bonded to the Zn²⁺ ions, thus, these Cl⁻ ions subsequently form H-bonding interactions with C₁-H groups in the cellobiose as well as C₃-H, C₅-H and C₆-H moieties, leading to selectively compete or wrap H-bond of cellulose itself. It also adjusts the amphiphilicity of the solvent, thereby increasing the ability to dissolve cellulose. At the same time, Zn²⁺ ions form coordination bonds with the oxygen atoms in C₆-OH groups in the cellobiose (ρ = 0.0458 au, ∇²ρ = 0.2021 au) and water molecules form H-bonds with the cellobiose, which also facilitate the cellulose to dissolve. Conclusion In summary, with the assistance of DFT calculations, a new solvent comprising zinc chloride, water and phosphoric acid (at molar ratio of 1:3:0.6) was successfully designed for the room temperature dissolution of cellulose. The data show that ZnCl2·3H2O and H3PO4 produce a new DES with strong H-bond donor-acceptor properties in which with water acts as an intermediate mediator to provide polar environment and avoid cellulose hydrolysis. This solvent has a protonation property and a characteristic of both having strong H-bonding acidity and basicity to achieve in efficiently dissolving cellulose (15 wt%). The newly developed solvent also has excellent universality, which can successfully dissolve the cellulose from various sources (e.g., microcrystalline, pulp cellulose, wood cellulose and cotton linter) at room temperature. This dissolution process did not phosphorylate the cellulose, although the cellulose recovered from solution showed a change in crystal structure from type I to II. Results and discussion 3.1. Designing a H-bond molecular scissors solvent The dissolution of cellulose depends on the free energy change in the mixed system, and this value is the sum of enthalpy and entropy changes. The driving force for dissolution is always an increase in the absolute value of entropy (Zhang et al., 2019). Entropy-driven dissolution reactions are of theoretical importance because free energy is the driving force for chemical changes. Therefore the interaction energy of cellobiose (a simple model for cellulose) was first analyzed by DFT calculations. The theoretical H-bonding interaction energy between cellobiose units was determined to be –15.05 kcal mol⁻¹ (Supplementary Fig. S1), while the glucosidic bond dissociation energy of cellobiose was up to 138.08 kcal mol⁻¹ (Fig. 1A). Ishida previously calculated the intermolecular interaction energies of cellulose at 25 °C, including the effects of reducing end groups, internal groups and non-reducing end groups in the gas phase as well as in water and ionic liquids, and obtained values in the range of –16.8 to –25.5 kcal mol⁻¹ (Ishida, 2020). The criterion for selecting solvents was that the interaction energy between the solvent and cellobiose should be greater than that between the cellobiose units but should not exceed the glucosidic bond dissociation energy, so as to achieve an efficient dissolution and simultaneously avoid excessive hydrolysis (Cho et al., 2011). Considering the complexity of cellulose-solvent interactions, the lower limit of the interaction energy for efficiently dissolving cellulose should be higher than 25.5 kcal mol⁻¹. Three metal salt hydrates were evaluated for the synthesis of new solvents by DFT analysis, including the LiCl·3H₂O (symbolized herein as MS1), MgCl₂·3H₂O (MS2) and ZnCl₂·3H₂O (MS3). Three acids were also assessed: oxalic acid (A1), acetic acid (A2) and phosphoric acid (A3). The interaction energies of the combinations of these compounds were calculated by DFT (Supplementary Fig. S2) and are summarized in Fig. 1B, from which it is evident that only the H-bonding interaction energy of the MS3A3 pair met the criterion of being larger than 25.5 kcal mol⁻¹. The interaction energies between each solvent combination and cellobiose were calculated based on DFT (Supplementary Fig. S3) and are provided in Supplementary Table S1. The MS3A3 system had the highest interaction energy with cellobiose (−29.44 kcal mol⁻¹), indicating that it could be the most effective solvent according to the criterion of selecting solvent (Supplementary Fig. S4). The experimental observation on cellulose dissolution also confirmed that only the MS3A3 system was capable of effectively dissolving cellulose (Supplementary 4 Z. Tong et al. This result suggests that MS3A3 has more numerous dissociated hydrogen ions, facilitating to improve the ability of solvent to destroy intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonds within cellulose. Other com- binations of metal salt hydrates and acids are deemed to be either inefficient or only fit for high-temperature hydrolysis of cellulose. On this basis, the MS3A3 system was considered an ideal solvent to test the aforementioned hypothesis. The atoms in molecules (AIM) theory is often employed to quantify the H-bond interactions at bond critical point (BCPs) in terms of electron density (ρ, 0.002–0.035 au) and the Laplacian of the electron density (∇²ρ, 0.024–0.139 au). The ρ value indicates the bond strength while the ∇²ρ value indicates the bond type (that is, H-bond, ionic bond or van der Waals force). In our solvent, the hydrogen atom of hydroxyl group in phosphoric acid molecule can form H-bonds with Cl⁻ ion (ρ = 0.0386 au; ∇²ρ = 0.0752 au) with a distance of 1.995 Å (Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. S4). This promotes the release of Cl⁻ ions from the Zn²⁺ ions, such that the distance between Zn2+ and Cl- ions is increased from 2.464 to 2.801 Å. Simultaneously, the Zn2+ ions coordinate with the hydroxyl groups of the phosphoric acid. The resulting interatomic dis- tances are within the range of less than 3.5 Å over which H-bonding can occur. Fig. 1C and Supplementary Fig. S4 exhibit the topological graph of the MS3A3-cellobiose system by AIM analysis. Table 1 summarizes the ρ and ∇²ρ values for all BCPs between MS3A3 and cellobiose. The calculation results indicate that H⁺ ions are released from the phosphoric acid that forms strong H-bonds with O atoms in C₆-OH groups (ρ = 0.0811 au, ∇²ρ = 0.1382 au). Meanwhile, the distance between Zn²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions also increases to 3.793 Å, indicating that the Cl⁻ ions are no longer tightly bonded to the Zn²⁺ ions, thus, these Cl⁻ ions subsequently form H-bonding interactions with C₁-H groups in the cellobiose as well as C₃-H, C₅-H and C₆-H moieties, leading to selectively compete or wrap H-bond of cellulose itself. It also adjusts the amphiphilicity of the solvent, thereby increasing the ability to dissolve cellulose. At the same time, Zn²⁺ ions form coordination bonds with the oxygen atoms in C₆-OH groups in the cellobiose (ρ = 0.0458 au, ∇²ρ = 0.2021 au) and water molecules form H-bonds with the cellobiose, which also facilitate the cellulose to dissolve. In addition, the ρ and ∇²ρ values in the cellobiose itself both decrease, indicating that the MS3A3 is theoretically capable of dissolving cellulose and is superior to MS3 and A3 alone (Supplementary Table S3). 3.2. _Room temperature dissolution of cellulose using MS3A3_ The resulting MS3A3 solvent system has several advantages. Demonstrations of pilot production and recyclable dissolution In the process of industrial production of cellulose dissolution, the desired solvent must have the characteristics of recyclability, good universality, pilot production, high efficiency, and low cost. In the solvent system that we designed, the MS3A3 demonstrates excellent recyclability. Even after recycling, the MS3A3 maintained its high ability to dissolve cellulose (original solvent: 15 wt%; after 1 time: 15 wt%, Fig. 4A and Supplementary Fig. S11). After reusing the MS3A3 for five times, the dissolved ratio of cellulose was 5 wt%, indicating the effect of the H-bond molecular scissors of the MS3A3 was retained even after being recycled and reused. In addition, the maximum dissolution ratios of other cellulose feedstocks with different molecular weights were also assessed (Fig. 4B), and in each case the extent of dissolution was considered satisfactory (Supplementary Fig. S12). Although the DP of cellulose feedstock increased from 183 to 2243, the dissolution time and the viscosity of solution did not change greatly (Supplementary Table S7), which suggests the broad applicability of MS3A3 for dissolving various types of cellulose. Fig. 4C presents photographic images of a pilot production experiment of dissolving 550 g of MCC with the MSA-3-0.6 at room temperature, demonstrating its suitability not only in the laboratory uses but also at the pilot scale. The cost effectiveness and minimal energy consumption associated with dissolution using the MSA-3-0.6 solvent indicates that this system could compete with the NaOH/urea system and superior to many other solvents (Fig. 4D and Supplementary Table S8). All these results support that the new solvent has a very broad and quite optimistic application prospects. ## 4. Conclusion In summary, with the assistance of DFT calculations, a new solvent comprising zinc chloride, water and phosphoric acid (at molar ratio of 1:3:0.6) was successfully designed for the room temperature dissolution of cellulose. The data show that ZnCl2·3H2O and H3PO4 produce a new DES with strong H-bond donor-acceptor properties in which with water acts as an intermediate mediator to provide polar environment and avoid cellulose hydrolysis. This solvent has a protonation property and a characteristic of both having strong H-bonding acidity and basicity to achieve in efficiently dissolving cellulose (15 wt%). The newly developed solvent also has excellent universality, which can successfully dissolve the cellulose from various sources (e.g., microcrystalline, pulp cellulose, wood cellulose and cotton linter) at room temperature. This dissolution process did not phosphorylate the cellulose, although the cellulose recovered from solution showed a change in crystal structure from type I to II.
